warmup.text: This is the last week of By the Great Horn Spoon. Answer the question on the card first. Then set your lens. This week you hold all four at once: what happens, who it happens to, what makes you smile, and what it all means.

words.text: This week you look back at every root family from the unit, and you practice editing: catching spelling slips and fixing one kind of mistake at a time. In the game, you proofread a letter from Jack.

reading.text: Read Chapter 16, The Gravediggers. The partners reach Shirt-tail Camp, and Praiseworthy has to speak up fast. Watch what he says and why it works. Then try the Read Like a Writer box.

assignment.text: Three questions about Chapter 16. Then plan the ending of your own adventure. Write three notes: what happens at the very end, who your hero has become, and what your story means.

do: Read the four lenses.
Tap the one you will use today.
Keep it in mind as you read. You will use it at the end.
how.why: Good readers finish a book by holding all four parts of a story at once.
how.use: You will use it in reading question 1.

do: Tap the highlighted words in the first sentence.
Write the second sentence correctly in your reading journal.
Tap See the Answer to check.
how.why: Fixing one kind of mistake at a time catches more of them.

do: Read the question.
Write 2 or 3 sentences in your reading journal.
Then go on to Word Study.
how.why: Thinking before you read gives you something to watch for.

do: Read the five root families.
Think through the questions, then tap See if you were right.
Write about three roots from three different weeks in the box.
how.why: Roots you already know open up words you have never seen.

do: Say each word out loud.
Tap each card to read its meaning.
Watch for the words as you read.
how.why: Knowing the words first keeps the reading smooth.

do: Read the editing checklist.
Fix the passage in your reading journal, then tap Now check your thinking.
Tap a sentence, then tap the pass that would catch its mistake.
how.why: Checking for one kind of mistake at a time is how editors catch them all.

do: Read the list of tricky words.
Do the task in your reading journal.
Tap a word, then tap Spelled correctly or Misspelled.
how.why: A few words cause most spelling mistakes. Learn those and your writing gets cleaner fast.

do: Read the reading focus below.
Open your book and read Chapter 16.
Then do the Read Like a Writer box and the Virtue Watch at the end of this tab.
how.why: The pause boxes are places to stop and think while you read.

do: Read today's step.
Write your three notes in the box.
Don't write the ending yet.
how.why: A strong ending ties together what happened, who your hero became and what the story means.

glossary.meaning: the big idea a story is about, like courage or what really matters
the main part of a word that carries its meaning, often from Latin

miss.recieve: Not quite. It is i before e except after c: receive.
miss.occured: occur + ed: the r doubles because you say oc-CUR. occurred.
miss.embarass: Two r's and two s's: embarrass.
miss.definitely: definite + ly. You can see finite inside it.
miss.separate: There's a rat in separate: sep-a-rate.

game.title: Jack's Letter Home
game.sub: This week's word game · 6 lines today
game.look: This letter is made up for the game, the way Jack writes letters home in Chapters 2 and 3. Every line has one misspelled word. Tap it, then tap the right spelling to ink the line clean. A clean letter gets a wax seal.

do: Read the line of the letter.
Tap the word that is spelled wrong.
Tap the right spelling to ink it clean.
how.why: Proofreading means checking every word on purpose, the way an editor does before a piece is published.

game.greet: Dear Aunt Arabella, Constance and Sarah,
game.doneLine: Come back tomorrow for the next letter.

lines.text: Praiseworthy and I are [truely] well, though the fleas are not.
lines.why: true drops its e before -ly: truly.
lines.miss: true + ly: one letter of true drops.

lines.text: Our burro Stubb is a [valient] animal, when he wants to be.
lines.why: val means strong. valiant: strong and brave, with -ant.
lines.miss: Find the root val, then the ending -ant.

lines.text: I took the squirrel gun out alone, feeling a little [nervus].
lines.why: nerve drops its e before -ous: nervous.
lines.miss: nerve + ous: one letter of nerve drops.

lines.text: The man who pulled me out of a coyote hole was a retired road agent, which was a [suprise] to us both.
Our pouch of gold dust is not very [valueable] yet.
lines.why: value drops its e before -able: valuable. Same val root as valiant.
lines.miss: value + able: one letter of value drops.
Count the m's and the r's.

cards.title: Real history: the real Sutter's Mill
cards.intro: Old Cap Sutter's sawmill is real, and the miners' yarn in Chapter 16 is close to what really happened.

items.meaning: James Marshall was building a sawmill for John Sutter at Coloma, on the South Fork of the American River. That morning he saw flakes of gold in the tailrace, the ditch that carries water away from the mill.
Henry Bigler, who worked at the mill, wrote that day: “This day some kind of mettle was found in the tailrace that looks like goald.” The spelling is his own.

Marshall carried the gold down the Coloma Road to Sutter's Fort, where the city of Sacramento grew up later. The secret did not keep. By July 1848 about 1,000 people were digging around Coloma, and in 1849 the rush was on.

The valley was Cullumah, a home of the Nisenan people. By 1848 many Nisenan had died of disease and conflict with settlers, and some worked for Sutter. The rush that started here took most of their land.

In 1848 and 1849 California had no state courts yet. In some camps, crowds held quick trials of their own and hanged people with no lawyer and no judge, as the crowd in Chapter 16 means to do. Many of those trials were not fair. California's first state courts began in 1850.
The spot is now Marshall Gold Discovery State Historic Park. A copy of the sawmill stands near where the first one stood.

cards.note: Sources: California State Parks, Marshall Gold Discovery State Historic Park; California Historical Landmarks 530 and 748.

virtue.name: hope
virtue.title: Hope, or not?
virtue.intro: This week's virtue is hope: believing good things can still happen, and keeping at it when things look bad. Sort these everyday examples.

items.t: Your team is losing at halftime. You tell yourself the game isn't over and keep playing your best.
items.why: Hope keeps you trying while there is still time.

items.t: You don't try out for the play because you're sure you won't get a part.
items.why: Giving up before you start leaves no room for hope.

items.t: Your science project falls apart the night before. You fix what you can and bring it anyway.
items.why: You expect something good can still come of it, so you keep going.

items.t: You decide a hard book is too hard after one page, and you stop.
items.why: Hope means giving something a fair try first.

art.title: Sutter's Saw Mill
art.alt: A pencil and watercolor drawing of a river valley with tall pine trees, the wooden sawmill by the water, and small cabins and tents of miners.
art.look: William Rich Hutton drew Sutter's sawmill at Coloma on April 16, 1849, a little more than a year after gold was found in its tailrace. Look for the mill, the tall pines, and the tents and cabins of the first miners. In Chapter 16 the partners walk right past it.
